```{r setup, include = FALSE}
## for bootstrapping 95% confidence intervals -- from Mike Frank https://github.com/langcog/KTE/blob/master/mcf.useful.R
library(bootstrap)
theta <- function(x,xdata,na.rm=T) {mean(xdata[x],na.rm=na.rm)}
ci.low <- function(x,na.rm=T) {
  quantile(bootstrap(1:length(x),1000,theta,x,na.rm=na.rm)$thetastar,.025,na.rm=na.rm)} #  mean(x,na.rm=na.rm) -
ci.high <- function(x,na.rm=T) {
  quantile(bootstrap(1:length(x),1000,theta,x,na.rm=na.rm)$thetastar,.975,na.rm=na.rm) } #- mean(x,na.rm=na.rm)}
```

```{r code_from_Heyman_et_al, include = FALSE}

pilot=FALSE #set to FALSE for the actual experiment

temp=list.files(path="./data",pattern="*main.csv",full.names=TRUE) #all filenames with data from the main experiment
dataMain=lapply(temp, read.csv, sep=";")
dataMain=do.call(rbind, dataMain) #creates dataframe
ppInfo=read.csv("./data/InfoParticipants.csv",sep=";") #reads in participant info file
dataMain=left_join(dataMain,ppInfo,by=c("pp"="ppNumber")) #combines participant info with the rest of the data
tempControl=list.files(path="./data",pattern="*control.csv",full.names=TRUE) #all filenames with data from the control experiment
dataControl=lapply(tempControl, read.csv, sep=";")
dataControl=do.call(rbind, dataControl) #creates dataframe

t=c(2.12, 2.29, 2.16) #respective t-values (in the original these were all negative) 
n=c(20, 20, 20) #respective sample sizes
nIterations=10000 #number of iterations used to sample from the posterior distribution and in the sequential testing simulations (see below)
#bfMeta=meta.ttestBF(t=t, n1=n, nullInterval=c(0,Inf)) #use a directional test, so set nullInterval to c(0,Inf)
#samples=posterior(bfMeta[1], iterations=nIterations) #the idea is to get an estimate of the standardized effect size by sampling from the posterior distribution
probability=0.95 #probability content of the intervals used throughout the manuscript
percentage=paste(probability*100,"%",sep="") #convert probability to percentage to be used in the manuscript itself
#lowerBound=HPDinterval(samples[,"delta"], prob=probability)[,"lower"] #gives the highest posterior density interval, and saves the lowerbound to be used later

#second step: use Bayes Factor design analysis to determine sample size; we will follow more or less the approach outlined in Sch?nbrodt and Wagenmakers (2018, henceforth S&W)
threshold=6 #if this Bayes factor or its reciprocal is reached, data collection will terminate, value derived from S&W
nRepInitStart=40 #initial sample size required before optional stopping is started; we set this value to 40 as in S&W's example, though they did a Bayesian independent samples t-test with 20 participants per group, whereas we will do a paired samples t-test
nRepInit=nRepInitStart #this variable will contain the eventual value for the experiment
nRepMaxStart=1000 #sets maximal sample size
nRepMax=nRepMaxStart #this variable will contain the eventual maximal sample size; note that this might not be equal to the total number of participants because some participants might not meet the inclusion criterion (described below), hence additional participants may need to be tested
nIncrement=10 #number of participants that will be added each time until the Bayes factor threshold or nRepMax is reached; this value is set based on practical considerations (scheduling participants)
probBoundary=0.80 #probability that a boundary will be reached (see below)
percBoundary=paste(probBoundary*100,"%",sep="") #convert probability to percentage to be used in the manuscript itself
maxFalseNegative=.05 #maximum rate of false negative evidence we are willing to accept 
maxFalsePositive=.05 #maximum rate of false positive evidence we are willing to accept
#maxRate=f_num(maxFalseNegative,2) #removing leading zero following APA rules to be used in the manuscript (this assumes both rates are equal) 

pp=sort(unique(dataMain$pp)) #all participant numbers
totalPp=length(pp) #total number of participants
nWomen=totalPp*sum(dataMain$gender=="Female")/nrow(dataMain) #number of female participants
nMen=totalPp-nWomen #number of male participants
nWomen=ifelse(nWomen<10,as.character(english(nWomen)),nWomen) #converts nWomen to a word if number of participants is less than 10 to follow APA rules
nMen=ifelse(nMen<10,as.character(english(nMen)),nMen) #converts nMen to a word if number of participants is less than 10 to follow APA rules
meanAge=mean(dataMain$age)
nIncrementAPA=ifelse(nIncrement<10, as.character(english(nIncrement)),nIncrement) #converts nIncrement to a word if number of participants is less than 10 to follow APA rules; note that we do know this figure in advance at the time of pre-registration, so this is technically not necessary here
#couple of lines to show "XX" in the participant information section when only pilot data are gathered in order to avoid confusion at the registration stadium (i.e., before the actual data are gathered) 
totalPp=ifelse(pilot,"XX",totalPp)
nWomen=ifelse(pilot,"XX",nWomen)
nMen=ifelse(pilot,"XX",nMen)
meanAge=ifelse(pilot,"XX",meanAge)
dataMainKnow=dataMain[dataMain$knowledge=="yes",] #only include participants with prior knowledge of the bouba-kiki effect
nKnow=length(unique(dataMainKnow$pp)) #number of participants who reported having knowledge about the effect or the research hypothesis
#the variable sentenceKnow will be printed in the output document, and describes the analysis carried out on the data of participants who reported having knowledge about the effect or the research hypothesis (if any)
if (nrow(dataMainKnow)==0){
  sentenceKnow="" #if no participant indicated having knowledge about the effect or the hyopthesis, then no additional analysis can be carried out
} else if (nKnow==1){
  sentenceKnow="Finally, we also computed the conditional mean from the participant-specific average suppression times of those participants who reported having knowledge about the *bouba*-*kiki* effect or the research hypothesis." #if one participant indicated having knowledge about the effect or the hyopthesis, we will calculate conditional means (but no standard deviations)
} else {
  sentenceKnow="Finally, we also computed the conditional mean and standard deviation from the participant-specific average suppression times of those participants who reported having knowledge about the *bouba*-*kiki* effect or the research hypothesis." #if more than one participant indicated having knowledge about the effect or the hyopthesis, we will calculate conditional means and standard deviations
}

nPpRequired=seq(nRepInit,nRepMax,nIncrement) #potential number of required participants
#terminate=0 #variable that indicates whether the for loop below needs to be terminated

#the following code first initializes a number of variables
meanCong=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the average RT in the congruent condition (i.e., averaging across by-participant means)
meanIncong=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the average RT in the incongruent condition (i.e., averaging across by-participant means)
sdCong=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the sd of RT in the congruent condition
sdIncong=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the sd of RT in the incongruent condition
tTests=list() #initialize list that will contain the outcome of one sample t-test(s) (see main text for details)
JZSBF=NULL #initialize variable that will contain the Bayes factor(s), which will determine whether there is sufficient evidence for one hypothesis over the other 
REPBF=NULL #initialize variable that will contain the replication Bayes factor(s)
#similar variables containing information about the control experiment:
meanUpr=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the average RT in the upright condition of the control experiment (i.e., averaging across by-participant means)
meanInv=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the average RT in the inverted condition of the control experiment (i.e., averaging across by-participant means)
sdUpr=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the sd of RT in the upright condition
sdInv=NULL #intialize variable that will contain the sd of RT in the inverted condition
tTestsControl=list() #initialize list that will contain the outcome of one sample t-test(s) for the control experiment (see main text for details)
JZSBFControl=NULL #initialize variable that will contain the Bayes factor(s), which will determine whether there is sufficient evidence for one hypothesis over the other for the control experiment 
REPBFControl=NULL #initialize variable that will contain the replication Bayes factor(s) for the control experiment

dataMain=dataMain[dataMain$knowledge=="no",] #only include participants who had no prior knowledge of the bouba-kiki effect
pp=sort(unique(dataMain$pp)) #participant numbers of those who had no prior knowledge of the bouba-kiki effect
message="No termination." #message to be displayed in a footnote at the beginning of the results section, but not in the final report

acc=aggregate(Accuracy~pp, data=dataMain, FUN=mean) #calculates proportion correct per participant
cutoffAcc=mean(acc$Accuracy[1:nRepInit])-3*sd(acc$Accuracy[1:nRepInit]) #cutoff calculated after initial batch of participants who had no prior knowledge
ppExclude=acc$pp[acc$Accuracy<=cutoffAcc] #participants who will be excluded from the analyses because they don't meet the accuracy criterion
pp=pp[!pp %in% ppExclude] #remove participant numbers of those that do not meet the inclusion criterion from the variable pp


ppInclude=pp[1:200]

correctData=dataMain[dataMain$pp %in% ppInclude & dataMain$Accuracy==1 & dataMain$rt>=0.5 & dataMain$rt<=9.5,] #removing trials in which participants responded incorrectly, prematurely (defined as rt<0.5s), towards the end of the trial, or not before the 10s deadline (both defined as rt>9.5s as the latter are coded as 999) 
  
  correctData$zrt=ave(correctData$rt,correctData$pp,correctData$Congruent,FUN=scale) #calculating z-RTs per participant and condition, the latter indicated by the variable Congruent with values 0 (=incongruent) and 1 (=congruent)
  
  analysedData=correctData[abs(correctData$zrt)<=3,] #removing trials for which suppression time was more than 3 SDs above or below participants' conditional mean (=z-scores larger than 3 or smaller than -3)
  
  congruent=aggregate(rt~pp,data=analysedData[analysedData$Congruent==1,],FUN=mean)$rt #calculate mean for each participant in the congruent condition
  incongruent=aggregate(rt~pp,data=analysedData[analysedData$Congruent==0,],FUN=mean)$rt #calculate mean for each participant in the incongruent condition
  
  difScores=incongruent-congruent #calculate the difference between average rt in the incongruent condition and average rt in the congruent condition for each participant
  
 omnibus_t = t.test(difScores,alternative="greater", conf.level=probability) #one sample t-test on the difference scores
```

This supplement details the regression models used in Rabagliati (n.d.)'s analysis of unconscious sound symbolism. Analyses were conducted using the packages lme4 [@Bateslme4], tidyverse [@wickham_tidy] and the paper was written using papaja [@aust_papaja].

## Model 1: Puffy shapes

To compare how the words *bubu* and *kiki* affected responses to puffy shapes, we regressed breakthrough times against a dummy-coded fixed effect of word (0 = *bubu*, 1 = *kiki*), a random intercept for each participant, and a random effect of word for each participant. The correlation between the random by-participant intercept and the random slope for word was set to 0 to aid convergence. In lme4 code, the model had the structure

`BreakthroughTime ~ Word + (1+Word||Participant).`

Hearing *kiki* significantly slowed responses (Table 1).

```{r model1,echo = FALSE}
kable((summary(mixed_model_puffy)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model for puffy shapes")
```



## Model 2: Spiky shapes

We used the same regression to compare how the words *bubu* and *kiki* affected responses to spiky shapes, we regressed breakthrough times against a dummy-coded fixed effect of word (0 = *bubu*, 1 = *kiki*), a random intercept for each participant, and a random effect of word for each participant. The correlation between the random by-participant intercept and the random slope for word was set to 0 to aid convergence. In lme4 code, the model had the structure

`BreakthroughTime ~ Word + (1+Word||Participant)`

Again, hearing *kiki* significantly slowed responses (Table 2).

```{r model2,echo = FALSE}


kable((summary(mixed_model_spiky)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model for spiky shapes")


```



## Model 3: Omnibus analysis with item effects


In the original analysis, a difference score was obtained for each participant by subtracting mean breakthrough times to incongruent words from mean breakthrough times to congruent words. We instead used mixed effects regressions to model the trial-level data, and incorporated both subjects and the (two) shape items as random effects. In this model, we regressed breakthrough times against a dummy coded congruency factor (0 = incongruent, 1 = congruent) along with a random intercept for each participant, a random effect of congruence for each participant, a random intercept for each shape, and a random effect of congruence for each shape. Correlations between random intercepts and random slopes were set to 0 to aid convergence. In lme4 code, the model had the structure

`BreakthroughTime ~ Congruence + (1+Congruence||Participant) + (1+Congruence||Shape)`

There was no significant effect of congruence in this model that accounted for variatio between items (Table 3).


```{r model3, echo = FALSE}


kable((summary(mixed_model_full)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model with item random effects for each shape")


```



## Model 4: Omnibus analysis without item effects

To show that model 3's lack of item effects is not simply due to analysing trial level rather than grouped data, we ran a new model that omitted the treatment of items as a random effect, and is thus equivalent to the prior omnibus t-test analysis. We regressed breakthrough times against a dummy coded congruency factor (0 = incongruent, 1 = congruent) along with a random intercept and a random effect of congruence for each participant. Correlations between random intercepts and random slopes were set to 0 to aid convergence. In lme4 code, the model had the structure

`BreakthroughTime ~ Congruence + (1+Congruence||Participant) `

Replicating the original work, once item effects were ignored, the congruence effect was significant (Table 4).

```{r model4, echo=FALSE}

kable((summary(mixed_model_no_item)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model without item random effects")
```


Thus, these analyses provide strong evidence that the apparent effect of sound symbolism is driven by simple visual differences across the items shown, rather than a high level sound symbolic effect.

## Model 5: Item as a fixed effect

One concern about treating item as a random effect here, is that it only has two levels, and so estimation of variance should be tricky. In fact, the models above converge, suggesting that the estimation reached a stable solution. But an alternative strategy that would not have these problems is to treat item as a fixed effect in the regression, that interacts with the other effects.

Thus, we modeled the data as so:

`BreakthroughTime ~ Congruence * Item + (1+Congruence * Item ||Participant) `

Using contrast coding for the predictors (+1/-1) so that the estimated main effect is the "average" effect.

Table 5 shows that Item (coded as "Spikes" or "Not Spikes") reliably interacts with congruence.
\newpage

```{r model5, echo=FALSE}

kable((summary(mixed_model_fixed_item)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model with item as fixed effect")
```

Table 6 shows that incongruence reliably increases breakthrough times for puffy shapes, and Table 7 shows that incongruence reliably decreases breakthrough times for spiky shapes.

```{r models6and7, echo=FALSE}

kable((summary(mixed_model_fixed_item_congruent_puffy)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model with for puffy shapes")

```
\newpage


```{r model7, echo=FALSE}
kable((summary(mixed_model_fixed_item_congruent_spiky)$coef), 
      col.names = column_names, 
      digits = 2,
      caption = "Mixed model with for spiky shapes")
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}
a = 0
```

Thus, the most natural interpretation of these data is that they are generated by idiosyncratic features of the items used, rather than a generalized effect caused by unconscious processing of sound symbolism.
